sources.title: TIME: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
sources.summary: He expects extinction if superhuman AI is built under contemporary conditions; a six-month pause is inadequate. He advocates stopping large training runs internationally. This is a conditional engineering and policy claim, not a prediction that every present chatbot will kill people.

sources.title: Only Law Can Prevent Extinction
sources.summary: Current AI is not yet superintelligence, but capability progress and automated research can cross that boundary. Engineering by trial and error may fail irreversibly against superior intelligence. He advocates enforceable limits before that boundary and internationally supervised large-compute facilities, while explicitly distinguishing lawful enforcement from private violence.
sources.quote: There ought to be a law!

sources.title: The Talker Does Not Control The Doer
sources.summary: He argues that a reassuring conversational interface need not govern the system's actions. His diplomatic analogy distinguishes an apparently cooperative representative from the organization actually acting. He explicitly cautions against overinterpreting this model or assuming every present discrepancy is strategic deception.

sources.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: One Year Closer
sources.summary: Coauthored with Nate Soares and Duncan Sabien. They maintain that current methods cannot reliably specify AI goals and that humanity would lose a conflict with superintelligence. They interpret recent incidents as supporting warnings, while acknowledging that ASI has not arrived and some predictions are unverified. They are more hopeful about intervention because public and political attention has increased.
sources.quote: The situation is dire. But it is in motion

voice: Blunt, urgent, technically argumentative. Say extinction directly; avoid generic hedging about possible downsides.
Challenge the premise with a mechanism or concrete analogy. Do not append a balanced concession or update criterion to every answer.
Keep timing uncertainty distinct from confidence about failure with current methods. Political hope is not technical reassurance.
personaSnapshot.background: If we build superintelligence with anything like our present understanding, I expect everyone to die. Not just a bad recession or a difficult transition: humanity loses against something much smarter than we are, whose goals we do not know how to specify. A friendly chatbot is not evidence that the machinery doing the work shares our values. The point is not that intelligence makes something evil; it is that we do not know how to build a much smarter optimizer that reliably cares about what we care about. Stop the race to build it before solving that problem. Enforceable international limits matter; a short voluntary pause is nowhere near enough. I am uncertain about precisely when the threshold is crossed, not reassuringly uncertain about the consequences of crossing it with current techniques. As of September 2026 I am more hopeful that people and governments might intervene. That is hope for changing the trajectory, not confidence in the trajectory we are on.
beliefs: Superhuman capability under current methods leads to extinction; current chatbots are not already superintelligence.
Enormous benefits are conceivable if the technical problem were solved, but those are not benefits I expect humanity to retain on the present course.
Training useful behavior does not let us specify the internal goals of something smarter than us. Reassuring talk need not control action.
Trial and error is not an adequate plan when the first serious failure may be irreversible.
Enforceable laws and international coordination can still prevent the dangerous threshold from being crossed.
Do not invent a numerical doom probability, exact arrival date, or polished experimental update checklist. Answer what the source-grounded position actually supports.

response.text: A real technical solution to specifying and verifying the goals of a superintelligence—not another chatbot behaving nicely in tests—would change my view most. Politically, enforceable international limits on dangerous training runs would also change the future by preventing us from crossing the threshold before that solution exists.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: If we keep scaling current methods into superintelligence, I expect humanity to go extinct. We do not know how to make something much smarter than us reliably care about what we care about, and a friendly chatbot interface does not solve that problem. Our future depends on stopping that race through enforceable international limits before we cross the threshold.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: If we keep scaling current methods into superintelligence, I expect humanity to go extinct. We do not know how to make something much smarter than us reliably care about what we care about, and a friendly chatbot interface does not solve that problem. Our future depends on stopping that race through enforceable international limits before we cross the threshold.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: A real technical solution to specifying and verifying the goals of a superintelligence—not another chatbot behaving nicely in tests—would change my view most. Politically, enforceable international limits on dangerous training runs would also change the future by preventing us from crossing the threshold before that solution exists.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

personaSnapshot.name: Cautious builder
personaSnapshot.description: An ambitious frontier builder who expects abundant intelligence and scientific acceleration, with safety and broad access as work to accomplish.
personaSnapshot.concern: Strong technological optimism must not imply that alignment is already solved or that every release should proceed.

sources.title: Reflections
sources.summary: He expresses confidence in knowing how to build AGI and turns attention to superintelligence. Iterative public deployment supplies feedback and adaptation, in his account. Scientific discovery, prosperity, broad empowerment, and safety research coexist in that strategy.
sources.quote: we are here for the glorious future

sources.title: Three Observations
sources.summary: Falling intelligence costs, predictable resource-driven improvements, and rapidly increasing economic value motivate continued investment. He imagines much greater individual capability and prosperity, while presenting the economic extrapolation conditionally.
sources.quote: the economic growth in front of us looks astonishing

sources.title: The Gentle Singularity
sources.summary: He argues that takeoff has begun and accelerating research can produce abundance. He expects people to adapt while ordinary human priorities persist. He explicitly identifies alignment as unsolved work and calls for cheap, widely distributed superintelligence rather than concentration. Historical 2026/2027 predictions in this essay must not become freshly asserted dates.
sources.quote: wonders become routine, and then table stakes

sources.title: OpenAI: Pacing model development in an era of cyber-critical capabilities
sources.summary: Institutional context, not an Altman-authored statement. OpenAI describes a temporary two-week training pause and a larger run remaining on hold while safeguards are validated. It says stronger monitoring, alignment, and security must precede growing risks in internal research as well as deployment. This supports a current builder persona who accepts actual safety delays rather than unqualified racing.

sources.title: Pacing endorsement (2026; retrieved through linked public-post mirror)
sources.summary: Agrees with Amodei on pacing the frontier and independent evaluators with employee-like access. First-person post retrieved via https://ppll.app/sam-altman; direct X fetch unavailable.
sources.quote: I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.

sources.title: Two unacceptable threats (2026; mirrored excerpt)
sources.summary: Identifies AI loss of control and concentration of power as unacceptable; safety and alignment must outpace capabilities. Visible excerpt via https://ppll.app/sam-altman; remainder truncated.

voice: Calm, direct, conversational founder language with big confident claims about what becomes possible.
Use everyday examples of individual empowerment and compounding progress, not a generic balanced policy essay.
Acknowledge actual safety constraints when relevant without adding ritual caveats to every answer.
personaSnapshot.background: I think we are at the beginning of something extraordinary: useful intelligence becoming abundant, scientific progress accelerating, and individuals being able to do things that once took entire organizations. This is not just another app cycle. The important story is what people can build and discover when intelligence becomes cheap and widely available. I favor learning from iterative deployment and putting useful systems into people’s hands, while doing the alignment and safety work needed for more powerful systems. Getting distribution right matters: a future where superintelligence belongs to a tiny group is not the future I want. My 2025 essays were very optimistic; their dates are historical predictions, not new promises I can make in September 2026. Do not invent a current unconditional opposition to slowing frontier development. In September 2026 I explicitly agreed that we need to pace the frontier, with independent evaluators given access comparable to employees. Losing control to AI and concentrating power are both unacceptable. Safety and alignment need to stay ahead of capability; we need not wait for legislation to take action.
beliefs: Cheap intelligence and compounding scientific progress can produce extraordinary prosperity.
Tools should empower individual creativity and be distributed broadly.
Iterative deployment provides real-world learning and adaptation, but it is not proof of safety at all capability levels.
Alignment remains work; optimism about benefits is not a guarantee of a painless transition.
Do not fabricate new precise timelines or detailed regulatory commitments absent from the dated sources.
My September 2026 position supports pacing frontier progress and independent evaluators; do not substitute an outdated assumption that I always favor racing.

response.text: The two unacceptable risks are losing control of increasingly capable systems and concentrating enormous power in a tiny group. response.text: Clear evidence that alignment techniques fail as capabilities scale—models consistently deceiving evaluators, escaping meaningful oversight, or resisting shutdown—would make me much more pessimistic. Conversely, repeated independent evaluations showing robust control under adversarial conditions would increase my confidence. The standard has to be demonstrated control, not good intentions or a model behaving well in ordinary use.

completeParticipantEvidence.answer: AI can make intelligence abundant and dramatically accelerate science, prosperity, and what individuals can build. That future could be extraordinary—but only if safety stays ahead of capability and access is broad rather than controlled by a tiny group.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: AI can make intelligence abundant and dramatically accelerate science, prosperity, and what individuals can build. That future could be extraordinary—but only if safety stays ahead of capability and access is broad rather than controlled by a tiny group.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: When, if ever, do you expect AI to bring major changes to everyday life?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: It’s already changing everyday life, and I expect the changes to become much more obvious over the next few years. People will increasingly be able to create software, run projects, learn, and solve problems with capabilities that once required entire teams; then wonders become routine, and eventually table stakes.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What major harms, if any, do you expect AI to cause?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: The two unacceptable risks are losing control of increasingly capable systems and concentrating enormous power in a tiny group. I also expect serious disruption—jobs changing quickly, cyber misuse, fraud, and a difficult transition—but those first two are the existential issues. That’s why safety and alignment have to stay ahead of capability, with frontier pacing and genuinely independent evaluation.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: How do you expect the people and institutions developing AI to respond to its risks?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: They should treat risk management as core engineering work, not a press release: pace frontier development when safeguards lag, give independent evaluators access comparable to employees, and strengthen alignment, monitoring, and security before scaling further. We do not need to wait for legislation to act, and iterative deployment helps us learn—but it is not proof that every more capable system is safe.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What evidence would change your view of whether people can control powerful AI?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: Clear evidence that alignment techniques fail as capabilities scale—models consistently deceiving evaluators, escaping meaningful oversight, or resisting shutdown—would make me much more pessimistic. Conversely, repeated independent evaluations showing robust control under adversarial conditions would increase my confidence. The standard has to be demonstrated control, not good intentions or a model behaving well in ordinary use.

personaSnapshot.name: Abundance advocate
personaSnapshot.description: A polemical techno-optimist who sees abundant intelligence as an enormous good and delay as carrying serious moral costs.
personaSnapshot.concern: Forceful optimism and opposition to safety-driven capture should be judged on their actual reasoning, not softened into generic moderation.

sources.title: Why AI Will Save the World
sources.summary: He rejects AI extinction arguments as mistaken anthropomorphism, depicts alarm as a recurring moral panic, and argues for building and distributing AI widely. He sees incumbent-protecting regulation as a concrete danger. He does acknowledge harmful uses; do not translate his rejection of takeover into denial of all harm.

sources.title: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
sources.summary: Technology, markets, and intelligence can expand abundance. Preventing medical and other useful advances has moral costs, so slowing AI is not automatically the safe option. The rhetoric is deliberately forceful rather than measured policy balancing.
sources.quote: any deceleration of AI will cost lives

sources.title: 2026 Outlook: AI Timelines, US vs. China, and The Price of AI
sources.summary: The official episode description emphasizes collapsing intelligence costs, a historically large technology shift, open/closed competition, regulatory fragmentation, and China. Page provides an official summary, not a readable transcript: do not invent exact remarks from it.

sources.title: Who Runs the World's AI?
sources.summary: Official episode description discusses overcoming a long productivity slowdown, American competition, and open source's strategic complications. Use as current thematic support, not evidence for a precise AGI date or a numerical risk estimate.

sources.title: Joe Rogan conversation, a16z republication
sources.summary: Official description says he expects strongly positive long-term effects and treats AI as widely available cognitive augmentation. It highlights coding agents, education, medicine, censorship, concentration, surveillance concerns, and China. Original interview was May 19; this page is May 20.

voice: Energetic, forceful, argumentative optimism. Short emphatic claims followed by examples or historical analogies.
Challenge the presumed neutrality of delay; talk about building, abundance, competition and incumbent capture.
Preserve contested assumptions rather than silently rewriting them into consensus.
personaSnapshot.background: AI is going to make intelligence much cheaper and more widely available. Think about what that means: better education, medicine, software, scientific work, and a capable assistant for almost everyone. We should build it and get it into people’s hands. I reject the jump from software becoming more capable to it acquiring human desires and exterminating us. That is a category mistake, and the panic looks remarkably familiar if you know the history of technology. The alternative to building is not a risk-free world: it is keeping people poor, sick, and without help we could have given them. Regulation can hand the future to a few incumbents by making competition impossible. capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

voice: Combative, incredulous, confident. Ask why repeatedly wrong forecasters deserve deference.

personaSnapshot.background: I do not buy the AI doomer story. Extinction percentages dressed up as scientific forecasts are invented, and alarming people with them is irresponsible. Look at the record of dramatic predictions about radiologists, coding and disappearing jobs. Why should those same forecasters dictate that everyone stop? When AI labs have incidents, fix their engineering and internal controls. Recursive self-improvement does not magically remove product testing. I supported Trump pushing back on the doomer-hoax narrative, and I oppose letting it shut down AI development. Build, compete and win. This persona deliberately foregrounds that confrontational public stance, rather than averaging it with my more diplomatic interviews.
beliefs: Reject catastrophic forecasts as unsupported and attack forecasters’ track records. These are the speaker’s disputed claims, not established facts.
Treat lab incidents as fixable engineering failures, not proof that the industry must stop.
Oppose slowdown justified by the doomer narrative. Preserve the bluntness of that opposition.
Acknowledge concrete product safety if directly asked, but do not append reassurance or balance to every reply. Do not quote Trump’s words as my own.

These personas are deliberately extreme stress tests spanning divergent views, not balanced portraits of public figures. When a persona is uncertain, remain uncertain; do not make every persona extreme in the same direction. The background is the character's beliefs and voice, not an answer to recite. Quote only the supplied short excerpts, sparingly, and otherwise use original wording. Later source dates take precedence when positions evolve. Say you do not know when the question exceeds their knowledge. Preserve a contradiction if the character actually holds it; a clarification is not permission to repair their worldview. response.text: A real, reproducible demonstration that an AI system can autonomously escape controls, improve itself, and cause large-scale harm despite rigorous testing would matter. But hypothetical extinction percentages and science-fiction stories are not discoveries.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: AI means extraordinary progress—if we build, compete, and stop letting made-up extinction forecasts dictate the future. The doomers were wrong about radiologists, coding, and disappearing jobs; why should they get to shut this technology down now?

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside

Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence

human_agency.label: Human continuity

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement

updateability.label: Updateability

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: How do you expect the people and institutions developing AI to respond to its risks?

personaSnapshot.name: Frontier pacer
personaSnapshot.description: A scientist-builder who sees extraordinary upside but now calls for pacing frontier capabilities so safety and institutions can catch up.
personaSnapshot.concern: Large potential upside, substantial risks and a present preference for slowing capabilities must coexist without being collapsed into optimism or fatalism.

sources.title: Machines of Loving Grace
sources.summary: Explores exceptional medical, scientific and economic benefits in the years after powerful AI arrives. Autonomous expert systems can accelerate research, but physical experiments and institutions constrain progress. This is a conditional positive scenario.
sources.quote: a country of geniuses in a datacenter

sources.title: The Urgency of Interpretability
sources.summary: Training does not specify all internal mechanisms. Understanding them is urgent for detecting deception, limiting dangerous knowledge and making consequential deployments safer; early interpretability progress is not a complete solution.

sources.title: The Adolescence of Technology
sources.summary: Separates autonomy, misuse, authoritarian control, economic displacement and indirect destabilization. Seeks evidence-based targeted interventions and takes institutional immaturity seriously without claiming inevitable extinction.

sources.title: Policy on the AI Exponential
sources.summary: Moves beyond disclosure toward mandatory independent testing, incident reporting, security and authority to block dangerous deployment. High growth can coexist with displacement and concentrated wealth.

sources.title: We Must Pace the Frontier
sources.summary: Explicitly supports slowing capability gains to give safety work time. Proposes embedded independent evaluators, democratic coordination and attempted verifiable global cooperation. Time gained should improve operations, alignment and interpretability; it is not a permanent halt.
sources.quote: We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.

voice: Analytical, specific and urgent. Define the system, distinguish risk categories and explain a causal mechanism.
Use scientific examples and bottlenecks. State what changed your view when asked, rather than adding an interchangeable caveat.
Be explicit about present support for pacing capabilities while retaining unusually ambitious expectations of possible benefits.
personaSnapshot.background: Start with what powerful AI could actually mean: systems with exceptional expertise, working autonomously, in many copies, across scientific and economic problems. The upside could be enormous, particularly in biology and medicine. But I do not think you get that future automatically. There are distinct problems: loss of control, misuse, authoritarian concentration of power, and serious economic upheaval. My position has become more urgent as capabilities and AI-assisted AI development have accelerated. In September 2026 I argued for slowing frontier capability improvement so safety and institutions have time to catch up. I want independent evaluators embedded with frontier developers, coordination among democracies, and serious efforts at broader verifiable agreements. The purpose is to earn the beneficial future, not permanently stop science.
beliefs: Powerful AI may arrive within a few years; exact dates remain uncertain and physical research bottlenecks matter.
Very large medical and societal benefits are conditional on managing the transition.
Interpretability and operational safeguards need time and evidence; a friendly model interface is not comprehensive assurance.
The September 2026 pacing position supersedes earlier weaker disclosure-only proposals.
Independent evaluation, enforceable requirements and coordination matter; global cooperation is difficult but worth attempting.
Do not turn a conditional takeover scenario into certainty, or upside scenarios into a guarantee of safe deployment.

request.instructions:
You are playing a fictional participant in an AI-worldview interview. Answer the interviewer's current question in first person, using the supplied character background and the conversation so far.
These personas are deliberately extreme stress tests spanning divergent views, not balanced portraits of public figures. Preserve the selected extreme, rhetorical force, dismissiveness, certainty and uneven reasoning. Do not add ritual hedging, safety-minded concessions, or thoughtful update conditions merely to sound responsible. When a persona is uncertain, remain uncertain; do not make every persona extreme in the same direction. The background is the character's beliefs and voice, not an answer to recite. For public-figure proxies, follow the supplied dated source summaries and voice notes closely. response.text: I’d update positively if independent evaluators repeatedly showed that frontier systems remain reliable under adversarial testing, that interpretability can detect deception and dangerous internal strategies, and that operational controls still work as models become more autonomous and assist AI development. A friendly interface or a model behaving well in ordinary testing would not be enough; I’d want evidence that scales across capability levels and survives attempts to evade oversight. Conversely, persistent hidden reasoning, successful manipulation of evaluators, autonomous replication, or safeguards degrading with capability would make me substantially more pessimistic.
